lesson.title: When New Learning Erases the Old
lesson.summary: Retroactive interference is the mirror image of proactive interference: newly learned information reaches backward in time and disrupts recall of information learned earlier, such as struggling to remember your childhood phone number after years of using new ones.
lesson.body:
Retroactive interference is the mirror image of proactive interference covered in the previous chapter. Instead of old material reaching forward to disrupt new learning, retroactive interference happens when newly learned material reaches backward in time and disrupts your ability to recall something you learned earlier. The direction of interference is reversed, but the underlying idea, that similar memories compete with each other for retrieval, is the same.

A common everyday example is address and phone number memory. Someone who has lived in several homes over the years often finds that the details of an old address, one they knew perfectly at the time, become oddly difficult to recall clearly once they have lived somewhere new for a while. The new address has not erased the old one from storage, but the newer, more recently used information interferes with easy access to the older information whenever both compete for the same retrieval pathway. Classic laboratory studies used a similar logic with word lists: participants who learned a second list of related material after an initial list tended to show worse recall of that first list compared to participants who did not learn any interfering second list in between, even though both groups had the same amount of time pass since learning the original list.

The proposed mechanism is much the same as with proactive interference: memories that share overlapping features or retrieval cues end up competing with one another rather than sitting in neatly separated storage compartments. When the more recently and often more strongly encoded material shares those same cues, it tends to win the competition, making the older memory harder, though usually not impossible, to access.

This idea has serious real world stakes in contexts like eyewitness memory. If a witness to an event is later exposed to new information, from a conversation with another witness, from media coverage, or from suggestive questioning, that new information can interfere with accurate recall of the original event, sometimes blending with or displacing the original memory. This overlaps closely with a more specific and well studied phenomenon called the misinformation effect, covered later in this unit, where misleading post event details do not just interfere with memory but can actually become incorporated into a person's account of what they saw.

Taken together, proactive and retroactive interference push back against a common but mistaken intuition that forgetting mainly means a memory trace fading away or getting erased like a scratched recording. Much of what we experience as forgetting is really competition between memories that are still present in some form, fighting for the same limited retrieval pathways, which is a considerably more active and dynamic picture of memory than a simple decay model would suggest.
